title: Searching with grep 🔍
description: Find patterns like a detective. Use grep, regex, and its most useful flags.

slides.title: grep: Global Regular Expression Print 🌐
slides.content:
## The Search Engine of the Terminal

`grep` searches through text for lines matching a pattern (regex).

Basic syntax: `grep pattern file`

If you don't specify a file, grep reads from stdin – perfect for pipes.

Common patterns: plain text, or regular expressions for flexible matching.

quizData.question: What does `grep hello file.txt` output?

options.text: All lines that contain the word 'hello'

quizData.explanation: By default, grep prints every line matching the pattern.

slides.title: Essential grep Flags 🏷️
slides.content:
## Supercharge Your Search

- `-i` : case‑insensitive.
- `-v` : invert – show lines NOT matching.
- `-r` / `-R` : recursive directory search.
- `-n` : show line numbers.
- `-c` : count matches instead of printing.
- `-l` : list filenames with matches (not content).
- `-w` : whole word match.

quizData.question: Which grep flag shows only the count of matching lines?
quizData.explanation: `-c` prints the number of lines that match the pattern.

slides.title: Regex with grep 💡
slides.content:
## Unlock Pattern Power

`grep` supports basic regex by default (`BRE`). With `-E` you get extended regex (ERE).

- `.` – any single character.
- `*` – zero or more of the preceding.
- `^` – start of line.
- `$` – end of line.
- `[abc]` – character class.
- `\|` – alternation (or).

Example: `grep -E '^(error|warning)' log.txt`

slides.title: grep in Pipelines 🖇️
slides.content:
## Filter Command Output

`ps aux | grep ssh` finds SSH processes.
`dmesg | grep -i usb` looks for USB device messages.
`history | grep git` searches your command history.

Always use `grep` as a filtering stage in your pipe.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Use `grep -q` for quiet mode – it returns just an exit code without printing. Perfect for conditionals: `if grep -q pattern file; then ...`
